Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry o f Earth Sciences, Technical Report No. 21, pp 11-20
Technical Report of 23r d  Indian Scientific 
Expedition to Antartica— An overview
Srinivasan Jayaram
Expedition Leader and Station Commander
The Technical Report of 23r d  Indian Scientific Expedition 
to Antarctica (IASE) for the year 2003 -  2004 is poised at a poignant juncture 
of Indian Scientific Expeditions to Antarctica. As Expedition Leader and 
Station Commander of 23r d  IASE, it is indeed a good fortune to witness a 
paradigm shift from a change at the helm and a complete reorientation of 
the scientific programmes resulting in a major quality jump and value addition. 
As this report is being prepared and submitted, it is appropriate to highlight 
these changes and value additions put in place by the National Center for 
Antarctic Research and Ocean Studies -  NCAOR -  the mother of / umbrella 
of all scientific programmes in Antarctica -  and now, the Arctic too.
NCAOR is currently going through some overhauls in its decade long/ 
10-year long existence, to adopt to the new requirements of Polar science 
This also coincides with the coming into existence the Ministry of Earth 
Sciences, Government of India. This also heralds the significant scientific 
feat of leaping, as it were, from the Antarctic to the Arctic. A great deal of 
reorganization has already taken place in the last three years / two years 
across scientific programs, state-of-art Laboratory facilities and a strategic 
new Logistics Programme to meet new requirements and challenges. The 
emphasis on collaboration with young scientists / research workers for 
advancing the frontiers of Polar Science is only one of the several such 
paradigm changes taking place at this point of time.
Climate change and key related issues of B iodiversity and 
sustainability are by far the biggest issues the world is facing today. 
There is an unprecedented surge of international awareness about climate

change, energy, oil, food production, biodiversity and degradation of natural 
resources. NCAOR has clearly focused on these burning issues as there is 
a new urgency and stakes have become higher.
REPORT OF XXIII INDIAN ANTARCTIC EXPEDITION
The present report is a collection of scientific papers that have emerged 
from the scientific programs carried out during the austral summer of year 
2004 (January to March) followed by the polar winter of 2004 (April to 
December). In essence, the report pertains to work in continuation of the 
on-going programmes of the previous year, with some new additional 
programmes.
The scientific papers have been grouped under (a) Meteorology 
and Atmospheric Sciences; (b) Earth Sciences, Glaciology & Global 
Change; (c) Biology and Environmental Sciences; (d) Engineering and 
Communication; (e) Human Physiology and Medicine; and (f) Logistics 
Support. The multi-disciplinary nature of scientific programmes with their 
core participating organizations and supporting institutions are shown in 
the following table.
(a) Earth Sciences, Glaciology & Global

NGRI, GSI, SOI, NHO
(b) Meteorology and Atmospheric Sciences IMD, NPL, IIG
(c) Biology and Environmental Sciences BSI, NCAOR
(d) Engineering and Communication DEAL, EIL, SERC
(e) Human Physiology and Medicine DIPAS, CCRAS
(f) Logistics Support Indian Army (EME, ES.3); MI

SIGNIFICANT HIGHLIGHTS
Without falling into the trap of “first time” metaphor, there have been 
some new programmes with a freshness of approach and a historic visit by 
the Hon’ble Minister of Science and Technology to Antarctica.
(a) Earth Sciences, Glaciology & Global Change
The first ever reference gravity station at Indian Antarctic base in 
Maitri, was successfully established by National Geophysical Research

Institute (NGRI) Precise Absolute Gravity measurements for deformation 
studies were obtained. The most crucial requirement of maintaining a 
temperature within the range of 158 to 258 Celsius was achieved by 
installing auto-cut-off heater during Absolute Gravity measurements. We 
have also connected earlier gravity observations with AGM reference point 
and reoccupied five GPS stations of Survey of India by digital relative 
Gravimeter. Continuous magnetic observations were also made for 20 days 
and a magnetic traverse across litho units in Schirmacher area carried out.
A second team of NGRI earned out the on-going programme of work 
pertaining to: (i) Daily operation of the Seismological Observatory, (ii) 
Daily operation of the GPS Tracking Station at MAITRI, (iii) Storage, 
Preliminary Analysis of Data periodically, and (iv) Backup of the Digital 
Seismic Data and GPS Data in addition to regular checking of the Systems, 
UPS, Batteries and Power supplies, etc.
